screens.title: Digital Outputs and Inputs with gpiozero
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn a practical, object-oriented approach to Raspberry Pi GPIO using the gpiozero library. You will see how physical components such as LEDs and pushbuttons become simple Python objects with methods and events. We start by confirming installation, then walk through the classic blink program, explore BCM pin numbering, and learn how internal pull-up resistors keep inputs stable. You will write both polling loops and event-driven handlers that toggle an LED when a button is pressed. The chapter closes with a hands-on wiring and troubleshooting checklist so you can build the circuit and iterate quickly. This matters because gpiozero lets you focus on behavior — on and off, pressed or not — rather than low-level electrical details. A concrete example you will run is an LED on GPIO 17 that lights while a button on GPIO 2 is held, and then refactor it to toggle state on each press. Along the way we contrast immediate state checks with event callbacks and call out a common wiring mistake: forgetting that the button connects to ground and that the internal pull-up keeps the idle state HIGH. As you begin, think about how turning a physical action into a concise object method changes the way you design projects.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Digital Outputs & Inputs
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Digital Outputs and Inputs with gpiozero

A practical introduction to controlling LEDs and reading buttons using gpiozero's object model on the Raspberry Pi.

Orientation

You will install or confirm gpiozero, run small scripts that control an LED, read a button, and refactor polling code into cleaner event-driven handlers. Expect hands-on wiring and a short troubleshooting checklist so you can get reproducible results on your Pi.

In this lesson
Blink, button reads, and events
Coming up
Pull-ups and wiring checks
Explore Key Topics
Install
Confirm gpiozero or install with apt for Python3 on Raspberry Pi OS.
Output
Control an LED using LED.on, LED.off, or LED.blink methods.
Input
Read a button with is_pressed or assign when_pressed callbacks.
Visual Concept
LED object
LED(17) represents a physical LED wired to GPIO 17.
Button object
Button(2) uses an internal pull-up so idle reads are HIGH and press pulls to ground.
Key Takeaway
Think in objects: call methods for outputs, read attributes or attach events for inputs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these exercises you will be able to install and import the gpiozero library, create LED and Button objects, and wire a working LED-and-button circuit on a Raspberry Pi. You will understand BCM numbering so you pick the correct GPIO pin in code, and you will know how the internal pull-up resistor keeps a button input in a known state when it is not pressed. Practically, you will write and run two small programs: a blink script that demonstrates output control and a button-driven script that first polls the button state and then is refactored into event-based callbacks. Each objective includes a reason why the skill matters. For example, learning event-driven inputs reduces C P U usage and simplifies multi-input projects; knowing BCM versus BOARD prevents wiring errors and frustration. You will finish with a verified competency milestone: wire the LED to GPIO 17, wire a momentary button to GPIO 2 and ground, and write a script that toggles the LED on each press. This hands-on milestone confirms both wiring and code work together.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Practical Checklist

Practical Checklist

Follow these measurable steps when you wire and code.

1. Confirm installation

Run the apt install command if needed, or open Thonny and import gpiozero to ensure the library is present.

2. Wire the LED

Connect LED to GPIO 17 and the correct resistor to ground. Create LED(17) in Python and call on and off to observe behavior.

3. Wire the button

Connect one side of the momentary switch to GPIO 2 and the other to ground. Create Button(2) and test is_pressed to read state.

4. Test polling and events

Run a polling loop and then refactor to when_pressed callbacks to compare CPU usage and code clarity.

screens.title: Installing gpiozero and verifying your environment
screens.narratorSegment: Before you write any code, make sure your Raspberry Pi can talk to its GPIO pins through gpiozero. On modern Raspberry Pi OS, gpiozero is typically pre-installed, but if it isn't present you can install it with the package manager for Python three. Running the apt install command ensures the system packages and dependencies are configured correctly. After installation, open Thonny or your preferred editor and run a short import test to confirm that gpiozero loads successfully. This avoids time-consuming debugging later. A simple verification pattern is to open a Python REPL and type the import statement; if there are no errors, proceed to wiring. When you import, gpiozero will select an appropriate backend for your Pi model so you rarely need to configure low-level drivers manually. Finally, check that you are using Python three in your editor and that your user has permission to access GPIO. If the import fails, double-check that you used Python three and that your OS packages are up to date. These preparatory steps are practical and prevent many common setup problems that interrupt hands-on time.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Install & Verify
Definition

Install and verify gpiozero

A short process to ensure your development environment is ready for GPIO work.

Step 1 — Check preinstalled
Open Thonny or the terminal and try import gpiozero in a Python 3 session. No error means you can continue.
Step 2 — Install if needed
If missing, run sudo apt install python3-gpiozero to install the library and its dependencies.
Step 3 — Confirm Python 3
Make sure Thonny or your terminal is using Python 3 so the package resolves correctly.
Common mistake
Running the install with plain python instead of python3 can leave you with the package in the wrong interpreter.
Code check
sudo apt install python3-gpiozero

# In Python REPL
from gpiozero import LED
print(LED)
Why this matters
  • Verifying import reduces wasted time on wiring problems that are actually software issues.
  • The library picks a backend automatically so you avoid manual driver choices on modern Pi models.
  • Using Python 3 consistently prevents package confusion between interpreters.
Key Takeaway
Confirm imports and interpreter before wiring hardware to streamline the lab session.

screens.title: gpiozero's object-oriented model
screens.narratorSegment: gpiozero uses object-oriented abstractions so you write code that models physical components directly. Instead of manually configuring a pin and toggling voltage values, you create an LED object and call methods such as on, off and blink. This approach maps hardware behavior to readable method calls and attributes, which reduces code complexity and improves clarity for beginners. For example, LED(17) creates an object that controls the GPIO 17 pin; calling the on method sets the output HIGH and supplies current to the LED through your wiring. Similarly, Button(2) gives you an is_pressed attribute that reports the button state, and higher-level events such as when_pressed to attach callbacks. The object model means that you can swap components in code without changing pin logic: use the same method names across physical device types. A common misconception is that gpiozero hides electrical reality; it does not — you still wire resistors and ground correctly — but it encapsulates the pin operations so you focus on behavior. Try to think of components as nouns and methods as verbs: the code reads like instructions for the hardware.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Object Model
Core Concept

Components as objects

Encapsulate pin behaviour with device objects so your code maps to physical things you build.

LED object
LED(17) provides on, off and blink methods that abstract the pin-level writes needed to light an LED.
Button object
Button(2) exposes is_pressed and event attributes. gpiozero sets up recommended pull resistors for you.
Misconception
gpiozero doesn't remove the need for correct wiring; it simplifies code by wrapping pin operations in friendly methods.
Concrete examples
from gpiozero import LED
led = LED(17)
led.on()
# wait then
led.off()
Analogy
Think of device objects as remote controls for hardware: they expose the buttons you need rather than exposing internal wiring details.
Key Takeaway
Use device objects so your code reads like instructions to physical parts: clearer, shorter, and easier to maintain.

screens.title: The classic Blink program
screens.narratorSegment: The blink example is the classic first program for physical computing because it verifies wiring and software together in a simple loop. In gpiozero we create an LED object with LED(17), then use on and off calls separated by sleep to flash the LED. This demonstrates basic output control and timing. A typical blink script imports time only for delays; an alternative is to call led. blink which runs blinking internally until you stop the program. The manual loop gives you explicit control: you can change timing or add other interactions between on and off. A concrete example you will run is: create LED(17), set it on for one second, off for one second, and repeat. When you run this, you should see the physical LED blink. A common confusion is pin numbering: LED(17) refers to GPIO 17 in BCM mode, not the physical 17th pin on the header. Check your wiring mapping before concluding the code is wrong. Finally, using blink() can simplify quick demos, while a looping approach is useful when you need to interleave other logic between toggles.

keyIdea.title: Blink
keyIdea.text: Use LED(17) with on/off or blink to verify an output and practice timing and sequencing.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Blink Example
Code Walkthrough

Manual blink loop

A simple explicit loop shows how to change timing or combine other logic between toggles.

from gpiozero import LED
from time import sleep

led = LED(17)

while True:
    led.on()
    sleep(1)
    led.off()
    sleep(1)
Run this script and observe the LED flash every second. If it does not, re-check the wiring and pin numbering.
Key Takeaway
Use explicit loops for full control; use built-in blink for quick demos.
Simplified API

Using blink()

from gpiozero import LED
led = LED(17)
led.blink()

input("Press Enter to stop...")
blink runs in the background until you stop the program. This is handy for demonstrations and reduces boilerplate code.
Example scenario
Use blink() when showing hardware in a classroom. Use a loop when you want to sample sensors between flashes or react to inputs.

screens.title: BCM numbering vs physical BOARD pins
screens.narratorSegment: One source of confusion is pin numbering. gpiozero uses BCM numbering by default, which refers to the Broadcom GPIO numbers exposed by the chip. That means LED(17) refers to GPIO 17, not the physical 17th pin on the header. Some other tutorials use BOARD numbering, which numbers the header pins sequentially from the connector. The practical effect is that the same number can refer to different pins depending on the scheme. When wiring, consult a pinout diagram that shows both BCM and physical pin numbers to map the correct header location. A common mistake is to wire to physical pin 17 while the code expects GPIO 17; the LED then does not light and you might suspect software when the wiring is wrong. To avoid mistakes, pick one numbering scheme and stick to it. In Python you can also select BOARD numbering if you prefer that mapping, but BCM is widely used in Python examples and on the Raspberry Pi documentation. The key skill is verifying the mapping between the number you type in code and the physical pin you touch on the header.

keyIdea.title: Pin mapping
keyIdea.text: BCM refers to GPIO numbers from the chip; BOARD refers to physical header pins. Mismatches cause wiring errors.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › BCM vs BOARD
Comparison

BCM and BOARD numbering

Understand which numbering scheme your code is using so your wiring matches the software expectation.

BCM (chip GPIO)
References the GPIO pin as named by the Broadcom SoC. Example: GPIO 17 is LED(17).
BOARD (physical)
References the header pin location. Physical pin numbers differ from BCM names on many pins.
Common mistake
Mixing numbering schemes when following an online wiring diagram often produces silent failures.
Key Takeaway
Pick BCM for Python examples unless you have a diagram labeled with BOARD numbers and double-check the mapping before wiring.
Quick mapping example
If your code uses LED(17), find the header pin corresponding to GPIO 17. If you instead wire to physical pin 17, verify whether that pin is indeed GPIO 17 on your model — they are not the same on most Pi models.
Practical test
Temporarily run a quick script that sets a pin high and use a multimeter or a known-good LED to verify the header pin toggles as expected before finalising your wiring.

screens.title: Reading a Button with gpiozero
screens.narratorSegment: Reading a button is straightforward with gpiozero. Physically, one side of a momentary pushbutton connects to a chosen GPIO pin and the other side connects to ground. When you create a Button object, like Button(2), gpiozero automatically enables an internal pull-up resistor. This means the input reads HIGH when the button is not pressed and reads LOW when the button is pressed because the pressed switch connects the pin to ground. In code, checking the is_pressed attribute within a loop allows you to poll the button state and react accordingly. For example, a loop that prints a message when is_pressed is True and sleeps briefly between checks is a useful debugging pattern. The polling approach is simple to understand and reliable for single-input projects, but it uses C P U cycles when the sleep interval is short. A common wiring mistake is connecting the button to 3.3 volts instead of ground; doing so will produce reversed logic and may short the rail when pressed. Always wire one side to the GPIO pin and the other to ground for pull-up behavior to work as expected.

keyIdea.title: Button reading
keyIdea.text: Button(2) with internal pull-up gives is_pressed for simple polling, where idle state reads HIGH and pressed reads LOW.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Button Reading
Definition

Wiring and polling

Connect the switch between a GPIO pin and ground. gpiozero sets the pull-up so idle reads are HIGH.

from gpiozero import Button
from time import sleep

button = Button(2)

while True:
    if button.is_pressed:
        print("Button is pressed")
    else:
        print("Button is not pressed")
    sleep(0.1)
This loop prints the state and pauses to reduce CPU use. Short sleeps make the interface more responsive but cost more CPU cycles.
Wiring note
One terminal of the button to GPIO 2, the other to ground. gpiozero's internal pull-up keeps the pin at a defined HIGH when the button is open.
Common mistake
Wiring the button to 3.3V instead of ground reverses behavior and can short when pressed. Always route the other side to ground when using internal pull-ups.
Key Takeaway
Button objects save you from manually enabling pull-ups and provide an easy attribute for polling the pressed state.

screens.title: Polling vs Event-driven inputs
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common ways to respond to a button: polling and event-driven callbacks. Polling means your program periodically checks button. is_pressed within a loop and reacts when the value changes. This is straightforward and easy to debug, but it consumes C P U while sleeping frequently, and timing depends on the sleep interval. Event-driven programming attaches functions to events — for example setting button. when_pressed to a function — so your code executes only when the event occurs. This is cleaner, often more efficient, and scales better when you have many inputs. A concrete example: a polling loop prints the button state every tenth of a second, while an event-based program toggles an LED only when the press happens. Event handlers are good for responsive interfaces and conserving resources, but they require thinking in callbacks and handling shared state carefully if multiple events can run concurrently. A common misconception is that callbacks are magically asynchronous; they still run on the main thread by default, so avoid long-running work inside handlers. Use event-driven callbacks for UI-like responsiveness and polling for simple, sequential tasks or debugging.

keyIdea.title: Polling vs events
keyIdea.text: Polling checks state regularly; event-driven code responds only when events occur. Choose based on complexity and resource use.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Polling vs Events
Process Flow

Polling example

while True:
    if button.is_pressed:
        led.on()
    else:
        led.off()
    sleep(0.1)
Simple and deterministic, but the loop runs continuously and depends on the sleep interval for responsiveness.
Process Flow

Event-driven example

def toggle_led():
    led.toggle()

button.when_pressed = toggle_led

input("Press Enter to exit...")
Cleaner and efficient for multiple inputs; handlers run on events rather than on a repeating loop.
Misconception
Event callbacks are not automatically parallel workers; long-running work in a handler can block other callbacks unless explicitly threaded.
Key Takeaway
Use events for responsiveness and scalability; use polling when you need simple sequential checks or explicit timing control.

screens.title: Toggling an LED with when_pressed
screens.narratorSegment: A common, useful pattern is to toggle an LED every time the button is pressed. This example uses a small callback function assigned to when_pressed. The callback simply calls the led. toggle method to flip the LED state. Because the callback is only invoked when a press event occurs, the rest of your program remains idle or can perform other tasks without busy-waiting. The program typically ends with input to keep the script running in the foreground until you choose to stop it. When you wire and run this example, press the button and observe the LED change state each time. If the LED toggles too quickly due to mechanical bounce, you may observe multiple toggles on a single press; gpiozero often includes simple debouncing, but you can also add small software delays or use the when_released event to shape behavior. This event-driven conversion is efficient and results in clearer code for multi-input projects where many sensors and buttons may need distinct handlers. Toggling an LED with when_pressed means assign a function to button.when_pressed that toggles the led, giving a responsive, cpu-efficient interaction.. In practical terms, use a callback to change led state on each press. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Event Toggle
Code Walkthrough

Toggle LED on press

from gpiozero import LED, Button

led = LED(17)
button = Button(2)

def toggle_led():
    led.toggle()

button.when_pressed = toggle_led

screens.title: Internal pull-up resistors explained
screens.narratorSegment: A pull-up resistor is fundamental to reliable digital inputs. When a button is not pressed its input pin must still read a defined voltage rather than floating. gpiozero configures an internal pull-up resistor so the GPIO pin sits at a HIGH voltage when the switch is open. Pressing the button connects the pin to ground, driving it LOW. This change from HIGH to LOW is what Button. is_pressed reports in code. Understanding this electrical behavior helps you wire the button correctly: one side to the GPIO pin, the other to ground. A common misunderstanding is to expect is_pressed to be True when the pin is HIGH; with internal pull-ups, pressing usually pulls the pin LOW, but Button abstracts this so is_pressed will be True when pressed regardless of the underlying HIGH/LOW mapping. The practical benefit is stability: you avoid noisy or random readings when the switch is open. If you need the opposite wiring or an external resistor, there are ways to configure pull-downs or use lower-level input classes, but the internal pull-up is the simplest and safest default for momentary switches.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Pull-up Resistors
Definition

Why pull-ups matter

Pull-up resistors ensure the input reads a steady HIGH when the switch is open and cleanly reads LOW when pressed.

Idle state
Internal pull-up ties the pin to a known HIGH through a resistor so the value is stable when unpressed.
Pressed state
Pressing connects the pin to ground so the pin reads LOW. Button abstracts this so is_pressed is True on a press.
Common mistake
Assuming the raw HIGH/LOW maps directly to pressed/unpressed without understanding the pull-up can lead to inverted logic errors.
Simple wiring visual
GPIO pin —[internal pull-up]—> HIGH when open. Press connects pin to GND → LOW.
Key Takeaway
Rely on the internal pull-up for simple momentary switches and avoid floating inputs that cause unreliable behavior.

screens.title: DigitalInputDevice vs Button
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter references both Button and DigitalInputDevice classes. Button is the convenience class designed for momentary switches: it configures pull-ups automatically and provides easy-to-use properties and events like is_pressed and when_pressed. DigitalInputDevice is a lower-level, more general input class that lets you configure edge detection, pull settings, and behaviors explicitly when you need greater control. In many beginner projects Button is the right choice because it handles common details for you and reduces boilerplate. Use DigitalInputDevice if you need custom thresholds, different pull configurations, or finer control over how edges and events are detected. A practical example: a simple doorbell or pushbutton should use Button; a custom sensor that requires specific timing or analog-like debouncing logic might use DigitalInputDevice so you can tune parameters precisely. Avoid prematurely optimizing: start with Button to get working hardware quickly, then switch to lower-level classes only if the built-in behavior does not meet your needs. Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Hands-on Activity
Process

Wire, test, iterate

  1. Power down the Pi and wire the LED with a resistor: anode to GPIO 17, cathode to GND.
  2. Wire the button: one terminal to GPIO 2 and the other to GND.
  3. Power up and run the blink script to verify the LED wiring.
  4. Run the polling script to observe button.is_pressed changes as you press and release.
  5. Run the event-driven toggle script and press the button to toggle the LED state.
Troubleshooting
If the LED doesn't light, double-check BCM pin mapping and resistor placement. If button readings are noisy, confirm the wiring to ground and check for bounce-related multiple triggers.

# Blink test
from gpiozero import LED
from time import sleep
led = LED(17)
while True:
    led.on()
    sleep(1)
    led.off()
    sleep(1)

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Assessment

Formative assessment

Ask and demonstrate the difference between immediate checks and event handlers.

Task A — Polling

        print('pressed')

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn a practical, object-oriented approach to Raspberry Pi GPIO using the gpiozero library. You will see how physical components such as LEDs and pushbuttons become simple Python objects with methods and events. We start by confirming installation, then walk through the classic blink program, explore BCM pin numbering, and learn how internal pull-up resistors keep inputs stable. You will write both polling loops and event-driven handlers that toggle an LED when a button is pressed. The chapter closes with a hands-on wiring and troubleshooting checklist so you can build the circuit and iterate quickly. This matters because gpiozero lets you focus on behavior — on and off, pressed or not — rather than low-level electrical details. A concrete example you will run is an LED on GPIO 17 that lights while a button on GPIO 2 is held, and then refactor it to toggle state on each press. Along the way we contrast immediate state checks with event callbacks and call out a common wiring mistake: forgetting that the button connects to ground and that the internal pull-up keeps the idle state HIGH. As you begin, think about how turning a physical action into a concise object method changes the way you design projects.

By the end of these exercises you will be able to install and import the gpiozero library, create LED and Button objects, and wire a working LED-and-button circuit on a Raspberry Pi. You will understand BCM numbering so you pick the correct GPIO pin in code, and you will know how the internal pull-up resistor keeps a button input in a known state when it is not pressed. Practically, you will write and run two small programs: a blink script that demonstrates output control and a button-driven script that first polls the button state and then is refactored into event-based callbacks. Each objective includes a reason why the skill matters. For example, learning event-driven inputs reduces C P U usage and simplifies multi-input projects; knowing BCM versus BOARD prevents wiring errors and frustration. You will finish with a verified competency milestone: wire the LED to GPIO 17, wire a momentary button to GPIO 2 and ground, and write a script that toggles the LED on each press. This hands-on milestone confirms both wiring and code work together.

This second objectives slide gives a practical checklist you can follow while live-coding. First, confirm gpiozero is installed or run the apt install command; this avoids surprises in the editor. Second, wire a single LED to the Pi and create an LED object in Python to call on and off. Third, wire a momentary button between the chosen GPIO pin and ground, and create a Button object; notice that gpiozero enables the internal pull-up so you will see HIGH when idle. Fourth, practice both polling with is_pressed and event-driven callbacks using when_pressed so you learn the trade-offs. Each item is measurable: you can run a blink script, see the LED toggle, and observe printed messages from a polling loop or an event callback. This checklist is practical because it connects wiring, code, and observation. Keep the verified milestone in mind: toggle the LED on each button press to prove wiring and code are correct.

Before you write any code, make sure your Raspberry Pi can talk to its GPIO pins through gpiozero. On modern Raspberry Pi OS, gpiozero is typically pre-installed, but if it isn't present you can install it with the package manager for Python three. Running the apt install command ensures the system packages and dependencies are configured correctly. After installation, open Thonny or your preferred editor and run a short import test to confirm that gpiozero loads successfully. This avoids time-consuming debugging later. A simple verification pattern is to open a Python REPL and type the import statement; if there are no errors, proceed to wiring. When you import, gpiozero will select an appropriate backend for your Pi model so you rarely need to configure low-level drivers manually. Finally, check that you are using Python three in your editor and that your user has permission to access GPIO. If the import fails, double-check that you used Python three and that your OS packages are up to date. These preparatory steps are practical and prevent many common setup problems that interrupt hands-on time.

gpiozero uses object-oriented abstractions so you write code that models physical components directly. Instead of manually configuring a pin and toggling voltage values, you create an LED object and call methods such as on, off and blink. This approach maps hardware behavior to readable method calls and attributes, which reduces code complexity and improves clarity for beginners. For example, LED(17) creates an object that controls the GPIO 17 pin; calling the on method sets the output HIGH and supplies current to the LED through your wiring. Similarly, Button(2) gives you an is_pressed attribute that reports the button state, and higher-level events such as when_pressed to attach callbacks. The object model means that you can swap components in code without changing pin logic: use the same method names across physical device types. A common misconception is that gpiozero hides electrical reality; it does not — you still wire resistors and ground correctly — but it encapsulates the pin operations so you focus on behavior. Try to think of components as nouns and methods as verbs: the code reads like instructions for the hardware.

The blink example is the classic first program for physical computing because it verifies wiring and software together in a simple loop. In gpiozero we create an LED object with LED(17), then use on and off calls separated by sleep to flash the LED. This demonstrates basic output control and timing. A typical blink script imports time only for delays; an alternative is to call led. blink which runs blinking internally until you stop the program. The manual loop gives you explicit control: you can change timing or add other interactions between on and off. A concrete example you will run is: create LED(17), set it on for one second, off for one second, and repeat. When you run this, you should see the physical LED blink. A common confusion is pin numbering: LED(17) refers to GPIO 17 in BCM mode, not the physical 17th pin on the header. Check your wiring mapping before concluding the code is wrong. Finally, using blink() can simplify quick demos, while a looping approach is useful when you need to interleave other logic between toggles.

One source of confusion is pin numbering. gpiozero uses BCM numbering by default, which refers to the Broadcom GPIO numbers exposed by the chip. That means LED(17) refers to GPIO 17, not the physical 17th pin on the header. Some other tutorials use BOARD numbering, which numbers the header pins sequentially from the connector. The practical effect is that the same number can refer to different pins depending on the scheme. When wiring, consult a pinout diagram that shows both BCM and physical pin numbers to map the correct header location. A common mistake is to wire to physical pin 17 while the code expects GPIO 17; the LED then does not light and you might suspect software when the wiring is wrong. To avoid mistakes, pick one numbering scheme and stick to it. In Python you can also select BOARD numbering if you prefer that mapping, but BCM is widely used in Python examples and on the Raspberry Pi documentation. The key skill is verifying the mapping between the number you type in code and the physical pin you touch on the header.

Reading a button is straightforward with gpiozero. Physically, one side of a momentary pushbutton connects to a chosen GPIO pin and the other side connects to ground. When you create a Button object, like Button(2), gpiozero automatically enables an internal pull-up resistor. This means the input reads HIGH when the button is not pressed and reads LOW when the button is pressed because the pressed switch connects the pin to ground. In code, checking the is_pressed attribute within a loop allows you to poll the button state and react accordingly. For example, a loop that prints a message when is_pressed is True and sleeps briefly between checks is a useful debugging pattern. The polling approach is simple to understand and reliable for single-input projects, but it uses C P U cycles when the sleep interval is short. A common wiring mistake is connecting the button to 3.3 volts instead of ground; doing so will produce reversed logic and may short the rail when pressed. Always wire one side to the GPIO pin and the other to ground for pull-up behavior to work as expected.

There are two common ways to respond to a button: polling and event-driven callbacks. Polling means your program periodically checks button. is_pressed within a loop and reacts when the value changes. This is straightforward and easy to debug, but it consumes C P U while sleeping frequently, and timing depends on the sleep interval. Event-driven programming attaches functions to events — for example setting button. when_pressed to a function — so your code executes only when the event occurs. This is cleaner, often more efficient, and scales better when you have many inputs. A concrete example: a polling loop prints the button state every tenth of a second, while an event-based program toggles an LED only when the press happens. Event handlers are good for responsive interfaces and conserving resources, but they require thinking in callbacks and handling shared state carefully if multiple events can run concurrently. A common misconception is that callbacks are magically asynchronous; they still run on the main thread by default, so avoid long-running work inside handlers. Use event-driven callbacks for UI-like responsiveness and polling for simple, sequential tasks or debugging.

A common, useful pattern is to toggle an LED every time the button is pressed. This example uses a small callback function assigned to when_pressed. The callback simply calls the led. toggle method to flip the LED state. Because the callback is only invoked when a press event occurs, the rest of your program remains idle or can perform other tasks without busy-waiting. The program typically ends with input to keep the script running in the foreground until you choose to stop it. When you wire and run this example, press the button and observe the LED change state each time. If the LED toggles too quickly due to mechanical bounce, you may observe multiple toggles on a single press; gpiozero often includes simple debouncing, but you can also add small software delays or use the when_released event to shape behavior. This event-driven conversion is efficient and results in clearer code for multi-input projects where many sensors and buttons may need distinct handlers. Toggling an LED with when_pressed means assign a function to button.when_pressed that toggles the led, giving a responsive, cpu-efficient interaction.. In practical terms, use a callback to change led state on each press. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The practical benefit is stability: you avoid noisy or random readings when the switch is open. If you need the opposite wiring or an external resistor, there are ways to configure pull-downs or use lower-level input classes, but the internal pull-up is the simplest and safest default for momentary switches.

Let's close with the core concepts to remember. First, gpiozero models hardware as objects: LED and Button are simple classes with methods and events so you can write readable code. Second, gpiozero uses BCM numbering by default; make sure the pin number in code matches the header you wire. Third, the library enables an internal pull-up for Button objects so the idle state is HIGH and pressing the button connects the pin to ground producing a LOW reading. Keep these three ideas in mind as you build: object mapping, correct pin mapping, and stable input states.
